sentences: A single woman stands alone on silk.
In a Joseon world where portraits were reserved for kings and scholar-officials, Shin Yun-bok painted this unnamed woman on a large hanging scroll more than 114 centimetres tall.
The painter is better known by his pen name, Hyewon.
His father, Shin Han-pyeong, was a court painter who helped create the royal portraits of King Yeongjo and King Jeongjo.
Shin himself painted kisaeng and the townspeople of Seoul in bright colour and delicate brushwork.
Let's begin with her hair.
A towering black wig sits high on her head, and perhaps because of its weight, her head tilts slightly.
The hair is drawn in very fine lines, strand by strand.
Moving down to her face, we find small, delicate lips and a gaze turned gently downward.
She bows her head as if shy, so she never meets our eyes.
A few loose strands of hair fall beside her ears.
Notice the short, fitted jacket, with its deep purple collar and the long ribbons hanging from it.
This cropped jacket and billowing skirt were the height of fashion in late Joseon Seoul.
Tight above and full below, the outfit reveals the line of the body.
The heart of this painting is her hands.
With slender fingers, she toys with the tassel ornament and the ribbon of her jacket.
That small gesture brings time into a still image: hesitation, perhaps anticipation.
Below, a jade-coloured skirt gathered in many pleats swells outward.
An orange-red sash at the waist adds a small spark of life among the quiet colours.
The contrast between short jacket and full skirt completes her silhouette.
At the hem, the tip of a white sock peeks out.
Some read this detail as a heart that wants to stay hidden and yet cannot help showing itself.
Her demeanor is composed, but it cannot quite conceal the flutter within.
Full-length paintings of a single woman as the sole subject are very rare in Joseon art.
This work is regarded as the masterpiece of late Joseon portraits of beauties, and it was designated a Treasure in 2018.
Now look at the writing in the upper left.
Beside the figure, the artist wrote an inscription saying that he had captured the spring stirring in her heart and conveyed her very spirit with his brush.
Below it are his pen name and a red seal.
It is a quiet declaration that he painted a mind, not just a face.
Now step back and look once more at her fingertips and her lowered face.
What do you think she is hesitating over?
